title: ECMO-assisted valve-in-valve transcatheter aortic valve replacement following surgical aortic valve replacement failure in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus-associated libman-sacks endocarditis: a case report.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Libman-Sacks endocarditis (LSE) is a non-infective valvular manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), affecting 15-30% of patients with APS. Characterized by sterile vegetations predisposing to thromboembolism and valvular dysfunction, optimal anticoagulation and intervention strategies remain challenging, particularly with rapid prosthetic failure.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 63-year-old African American man with a 20-year history of SLE and triple-positive APS presented with cardiogenic shock five months after surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) for LSE. Echocardiography revealed severe bioprosthetic obstruction (mean gradient 79.6 mmHg, valve area 0.30 cm²). Given prohibitive redo surgical risk (STS-PROM 18.2%), he underwent ECMO-assisted valve-in-valve transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with a 26 mm Edwards SAPIEN 3 valve. Left ventricular ejection fraction improved from 25-29% to 55-59% at 4.5 months, sustained at 50-54% at 8-month follow-up. He remained stable on warfarin (INR 2-3), hydroxychloroquine, and rituximab under multidisciplinary care.
DISCUSSION: This case demonstrates diagnostic challenges differentiating LSE from bioprosthetic valve thrombosis (BPVT); a competing diagnosis that could not be excluded without histopathologic confirmation, critical limitations of DOACs in triple-positive APS, and feasibility of ECMO-supported TAVR as an exceptional rescue strategy. Rituximab was administered for refractory APS, though its independent contribution to the favorable outcome cannot be determined.
CONCLUSION: To our knowledge, this is the first reported ECMO-assisted valve-in-valve TAVR following SAVR failure in APS/SLE-associated LSE. It emphasizes multidisciplinary care, warfarin-based anticoagulation, immunosuppression escalation, and long-term surveillance for complex autoimmune valvular disease.

title: Synergizing Multiple Stress Induction and Mitophagy Blockade via a Single-Atom Piezocatalyst for Enhanced Sono-Immunotherapy.
abstract: Piezoelectric sonodynamic therapy (SDT) holds great promise in the treatment of solid tumors, but its efficacy is severely limited by the rapid recombination of charge carriers, the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), and the protective mitophagy clearance of tumor cells. Herein, we constructed a single-atom piezoelectric nanoplatform (HCQ@Ru@Cu3VS4-x) that synergizes multiple stress induction with damage clearance blockade. Through defect engineering, ruthenium single atoms (RuSA) are precisely anchored on the sulfur vacancies (SV) of Cu3VS4-x, establishing a strong metal-support interaction (SMSI). This structure not only reduces the bandgap and amplifies the ultrasound-triggered piezoelectric polarization effect to achieve cascade amplification of ROS production, but also provides multiple enzyme-mimic activities for TME remodeling. Moreover, the tumor-specific release of Cu ions triggers cuproptosis-mediated metabolic stress, while the co-loaded hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) specifically disrupts lysosomal acidification thereby blocking the mitophagy clearance pathway of damaged mitochondria. This lethal combination of mitochondrial damage amplification and restricted clearance pathways leads to irreversible mitochondrial dysfunction and triggers immunogenic cell death (ICD). In vivo evaluations demonstrate that this synergistic paradigm can not only eradicate primary tumors but also elicit a potent abscopal effect to suppress distant metastasis, providing a novel paradigm for overcoming immune tolerance and therapeutic resistance in complex solid tumors.
